question: What is the JUnit 5 test execution lifecycle?
title: JUnit 5 Test Lifecycle | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **JUnit 5 creates a new test class instance for each test method** (default). Execution order: @BeforeAll (static, once) → for each test: @BeforeEach → @Test → @AfterEach → @AfterAll (static, once). This ensures test independence.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of JUnit lifecycle and why it's designed this way
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking JUnit creates one instance for all tests (that was JUnit 4 default) — JUnit 5 defaults to PER_METHOD
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain @TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS) and when you'd use it to avoid static on @BeforeAll

sections.title: New Instance Per Test Method
sections.content: Default in JUnit 5: **PER_METHOD** — a new test class instance is created for each @Test method. This is why @BeforeAll must be static — if it weren't, which instance would it belong to? Order: `@BeforeAll` (once) → `@BeforeEach` (per test) → `@Test` → `@AfterEach` (per test) → `@AfterAll` (once). If a @BeforeEach throws, the @Test doesn't run but @AfterEach still runs.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Default: PER_METHOD — new instance per @Test
- PER_CLASS: @TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS) — one instance for all
- PER_CLASS: @BeforeAll can be non-static
- PER_METHOD: ensures test isolation — state resets per test
- Order: @BeforeAll → [@BeforeEach → @Test → @AfterEach] × n → @AfterAll
- Nested tests: outer @BeforeEach runs for nested tests too
- @BeforeEach on failure: @Test skipped, @AfterEach still runs
- @TestMethodOrder: control execution order (not recommended for independent tests)

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: JUnit 5 creates a new test class instance for each test method by default — this is the PER_METHOD lifecycle. The full order is: @BeforeAll runs once statically before everything, then for each test method @BeforeEach runs, then the @Test method, then @AfterEach. @AfterAll runs once after all tests. Because a new instance is created per test, @BeforeAll must be static since there's no single instance to attach it to. If I annotate the class with @TestInstance PER_CLASS, JUnit reuses one instance and @BeforeAll can be non-static — useful when setup is expensive.

By creating a fresh instance per test, JUnit makes it structurally impossible for instance fields to leak state between tests. You have to go out of your way to share state — which prevents accidental coupling.

question: What happens when a @BeforeEach method throws an exception?
title: @BeforeEach Exception Handling JUnit 5 | Java Fresher
direct_answer: **If @BeforeEach throws, the @Test method does NOT run, but @AfterEach still runs.** The test is marked as failed (not skipped). This allows @AfterEach to clean up resources even when setup fails — preventing resource leaks.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming the test is skipped rather than failed when setup throws
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the design rationale: @AfterEach always runs to prevent resource leaks, similar to a finally block

sections.title: @AfterEach Always Runs — Like Finally
sections.content: Think of the lifecycle as a try-finally: @AfterEach is in the finally block. Even if @BeforeEach throws, @AfterEach runs to clean up any partially acquired resources. The test itself is reported as **FAILED** with the exception from @BeforeEach — not SKIPPED. This ensures cleanup always happens, preventing resource leaks in cases like database connections or file handles opened in @BeforeEach.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- @BeforeEach throws → @Test does NOT run
- @BeforeEach throws → @AfterEach STILL runs (like finally)
- Test is marked FAILED, not SKIPPED
- Same principle: if @Test throws → @AfterEach still runs
- @AfterEach can also throw — both failures reported
- Design rationale: prevent resource leaks
- To fix: ensure @BeforeEach doesn't throw for valid test scenarios

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: If @BeforeEach throws an exception, JUnit skips the @Test method and marks the test as failed — not skipped — with the exception from @BeforeEach. Importantly, @AfterEach still runs even in this case, similar to a finally block in Java. This design ensures cleanup happens even when setup fails, preventing resource leaks. For example, if @BeforeEach opens a database connection and then fails, @AfterEach can still close it. In practice I make sure @BeforeEach is robust and doesn't throw for scenarios that should be testable — throwing in setup usually indicates a configuration problem rather than a real test failure.

question: What is @TestInstance and when would you use PER_CLASS lifecycle?
title: @TestInstance JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS) creates one test class instance for all test methods.** This allows @BeforeAll to be non-static and enables sharing expensive state across tests. Use it when setup is very expensive (e.g., starting an embedded server). Default is PER_METHOD.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing this annotation exists and always struggling with static @BeforeAll
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the tradeoff: PER_CLASS is more efficient for expensive setup but tests may share state — use carefully

sections.title: One Instance for All Tests
sections.content: By default (PER_METHOD), a new instance is created per test and all @BeforeAll methods must be static. With `@TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS)`: one instance for all tests — @BeforeAll and @AfterAll can be non-static instance methods. **Use case**: expensive setup like starting an embedded Kafka or database that you want to share. **Risk**: tests may share state through instance variables — if one test modifies state, subsequent tests see it. Mitigate with careful @BeforeEach reset.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- PER_METHOD (default): new instance per test — maximum isolation
- PER_CLASS: one instance — @BeforeAll can be non-static
- PER_CLASS use case: expensive embedded resources (Kafka, Testcontainers)
- Risk: shared instance state between tests
- Mitigation: reset mutable state in @BeforeEach
- @Nested tests inherit parent's lifecycle setting
- @SpringBootTest uses PER_CLASS internally for context reuse

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @TestInstance controls how many instances of the test class JUnit creates. The default PER_METHOD creates a new instance for each test, ensuring maximum isolation but requiring @BeforeAll to be static. PER_CLASS creates one instance for all tests in the class, allowing @BeforeAll to be non-static, and is useful when setup is expensive — like starting an embedded Kafka broker or a Testcontainers database. The risk is that tests share the instance state, so if one test mutates a field, subsequent tests see that mutation. With PER_CLASS I make sure to reset mutable state in @BeforeEach.

question: Can you control the execution order of tests in JUnit 5?
title: JUnit 5 Test Execution Order | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **By default, JUnit 5 does not guarantee execution order.** Use `@TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation.class)` with `@Order(1)`, `@Order(2)` on methods to enforce order. However, tests should be independent — ordering is a design smell unless you're writing integration scenarios.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of test ordering and the principle that tests should be order-independent
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing tests that depend on execution order — a sign of shared state that should be fixed
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note that needing ordered tests usually indicates a design problem — tests should be independent

sections.title: Ordering as a Last Resort
sections.content: JUnit 5 purposefully randomizes order (within a run) to expose tests that accidentally depend on each other. To enforce order: `@TestClassOrder(ClassOrderer.OrderAnnotation.class)` on a class, or `@TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation.class)` + `@Order(n)` on methods. Other orderers: `MethodOrderer.Random.class` (explicit randomization), `MethodOrderer.DisplayName.class` (alphabetical by display name). **Principle**: if you need ordering, your tests likely share state — fix the root cause.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Default: deterministic but not user-controlled (same run = same order)
- @TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation.class) enables @Order
- @Order(1): runs first, @Order(2): second, etc.
- Alternatives: DisplayName (alphabetical), Random (deliberate chaos testing)
- Needing order = design smell = shared mutable state
- Integration tests: ordering can be valid for multi-step scenarios
- @TestClassOrder: control class execution order in a test suite

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: JUnit 5 doesn't guarantee execution order by default, though within a single run it's deterministic. You can force order with @TestMethodOrder and @Order annotations. But I'd push back on the need for it — if tests must run in a specific order, it usually means they share state or have dependencies on each other, which violates the 'I' in FIRST (Independent). The right fix is to make each test set up its own state independently. Ordering might be acceptable for integration tests that simulate a multi-step user workflow, but for unit tests it's a red flag.

question: How do you use @TempDir in JUnit 5 for file system tests?
title: @TempDir JUnit 5 | Java Fresher Interview
direct_answer: **@TempDir** injects a temporary directory that JUnit creates before the test and deletes after. Use it for tests that read/write files — avoids manual temp dir creation and cleanup. Inject as `Path` or `File` parameter.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge of JUnit 5's built-in extensions for practical scenarios
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Manually creating and deleting temp directories in @BeforeEach/@AfterEach when @TempDir does it automatically
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that @TempDir ensures cleanup even if the test fails — a resource management advantage

sections.title: Automatic Temp Directory Lifecycle
sections.content: `@TempDir Path tempDir` — inject as test class field (shared across methods) or as method parameter (fresh per method). JUnit creates the directory before the test and deletes it after — even if the test fails. Example: test a `FileProcessor` by writing to `tempDir.resolve("input.txt")` and reading from the output. No cleanup code needed.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Inject as Path or File
- Class field: shared across all tests in the class
- Method parameter: fresh temp dir per test
- Auto-deleted after test — even on failure
- Use Path.of and Files API for modern Java file operations
- Avoids boilerplate @BeforeEach/@AfterEach for temp dirs
- Works with @BeforeEach to set up files in the directory
- Cannot be used with @BeforeAll unless PER_CLASS lifecycle

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: @TempDir is a JUnit 5 built-in extension that injects a temporary directory into your test. I annotate a field or method parameter with @TempDir and declare it as a Path. JUnit creates the directory before the test and deletes it after — including all contents — even if the test fails. This is much better than manually creating temp directories in @BeforeEach because cleanup is guaranteed and the code is simpler. I use it for tests that involve file reading and writing, like testing a CSV parser or a file-based configuration loader.

As a class field: JUnit creates one directory shared across all tests in the class
